Review: Units 21–26

Units 21.1, 21.6

Using "there is" and "there are"

Use There is for one thing and There are for more than one, to say that something exists. Make it negative with There isn't or There aren't. We often contract "there is" to There's.

There is a hospital. There are three hospitals. There isn't a school. There aren't any schools. There's a park nearby.

There is / There are

PositiveNegative
SingularThere is / There'sThere isn't
PluralThere areThere aren't

We use "any" with plural negatives and questions: "There aren't any schools," "Are there any schools?"

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. one hospital a hospital nearby.
  2. three hospitals three hospitals in this town.
  3. no school here a school in this village.
  4. no stores here (plural) any stores nearby.
  5. a contraction a park across the street.
  6. asking about hotels any hotels in town?
  7. asking about a bank a bank nearby?
  8. two restaurants two restaurants on this street.

Yes, there are three hotels near the park. There isn't a supermarket in the center, but there are two just outside town. There aren't many restaurants, but the few that exist are excellent.

Unit 22.1

Articles

Use a or an for one thing when it isn't specific, or when you mention it for the first time. Use the when the listener already knows which one you mean.

I work in a library. I work in the library on Main Street. She bought a book. The book was expensive. The sun is bright today.

a/an vs. the

ArticleUseExample
a / anfirst mention, not specificI saw a cat.
thealready known, specificThe cat is mine.

We use "the" for things that are unique, like the sun, the moon, or the internet.

Grammar practice: choose a, an, or the

  1. first mention I saw cat in the yard.
  2. already mentioned cat was orange.
  3. a unique thing sun rose early today.
  4. first mention, vowel sound She bought apple.
  5. specific, already known place I work in library on Main Street.
  6. not specific I need pen.
  7. already known Where is pen I gave you?
  8. first mention He has dog.

The cat looked hungry, so Mia gave it some food. Later, she read the book she bought. The pictures inside were even better than the cover.

Unit 22.8

Using "any" and "some"

Use some in positive sentences for an unspecified amount. Use any in questions and negative sentences.

Are there any hotels? There are some hotels. I have some money. I don't have any money.

any vs. some

Sentence typeWordExample
PositivesomeThere are some apples.
QuestionanyAre there any apples?
NegativeanyThere aren't any apples.

We can also use "some" in a question when offering or asking for something: "Would you like some tea?"

Grammar practice: choose any or some

  1. positive statement There are hotels near the station.
  2. question Are there hotels in town?
  3. negative I don't have money left.
  4. positive She bought apples at the market.
  5. question Do you have questions?
  6. negative There isn't milk in the fridge.
  7. positive We need more chairs for the party.
  8. offering something Would you like coffee?

Unit 23.1

Imperatives

Use the base form of the verb, with no subject, to give a command, instruction, or warning. Add Don't before the verb to make it negative.

Stop! Be careful! Open the door. Don't touch that. Turn left at the corner.

Forming imperatives

TypeFormExample
Positive commandbase verbClose the window.
Negative commandDon't + base verbDon't touch that.
Polite requestPlease + base verbPlease wait here.

Imperatives don't use a subject pronoun — we say "Stop!" not "You stop!"

Grammar practice: complete each command

  1. warn someone about danger careful!
  2. telling someone to stop right there!
  3. negative command touch the stove.
  4. giving a direction left at the light.
  5. polite request sit down.
  6. negative command forget your keys.
  7. instruction the door before you leave.
  8. base verb, no subject quiet in the library.

Reading practice

The lifeguard blows her whistle. "Stop!" she shouts to a boy near the deep end. "Don't swim past the rope," she warns him. "Be careful, everyone!" she calls to the group. A younger child runs near the pool. "Don't run!" the lifeguard says firmly. "Walk, please." Later, she reminds everyone, "Please listen for the whistle. When you hear it, get out of the water immediately." Everyone nods and follows her instructions.

Check your understanding

2. The lifeguard warns the group to be careful.

3. The younger child is told to run faster.

4. Everyone should get out of the water when they hear the whistle.

5. The lifeguard never gives any instructions.

Units 24.1, 24.7

Joining sentences

Use and to join two similar ideas. Use but to join two contrasting ideas. Add a comma before "but" when it joins two full sentences.

There's a library and a restaurant. There's a hotel, but there isn't a store. I like tea and coffee. She is tired, but she keeps working.

and vs. but

WordUseExample
andjoins similar ideasa library and a restaurant
butjoins contrasting ideasa hotel, but no store

Use a comma before "but" when it joins two full sentences: "There's a hotel, but there isn't a store."

Grammar practice: choose and or but

  1. two similar things There's a park a playground.
  2. a contrast The town is small, it is very friendly.
  3. two similar things I like apples oranges.
  4. a contrast He wanted to come, he was too tired.
  5. two similar things There's a bank a post office.
  6. a contrast The hotel is nice, it is expensive.
  7. two similar things We visited Paris Rome.
  8. a contrast She studied hard, she still failed.

The restaurants are excellent, but they can be expensive. We have a train station and a bus stop, so getting around is easy. The weather is usually sunny, but it can get cold in winter. Overall, it's a great place to live, and most people love it here.

Units 25.1, 25.4

Using adjectives

An adjective describes a noun. It can come before the noun, or after "to be". Adjectives don't change form for singular or plural nouns.

She is a busy woman. It is a busy town. The town is busy. It is busy.

Where adjectives go

PositionExample
Before the nouna busy town
After to beThe town is busy.

Adjectives never take a plural -s in English: we say "busy towns," not "busies towns."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. before the noun (busy) She is a woman.
  2. after to be (busy) The town is .
  3. before the noun, plural (busy) They have jobs.
  4. after to be (hot) The soup is .
  5. before the noun (hot) It's a day.
  6. after to be, plural subject (small) The rooms are .
  7. before the noun (small) We live in a house.
  8. adjectives don't change for plural nouns (big) I have three dogs.

Her apartment is small, but it's comfortable. On weekends, the city feels less busy, and Ana enjoys the quiet mornings. Her friend says the city is too busy for her, but Ana loves the energy.

Unit 26.1

Using "because"

Use because to give a reason for something. It comes before a full clause — a subject plus a verb, not just a noun.

I live in the countryside because it's beautiful. She is tired because she worked all night. We stayed inside because it was raining. He studies English because he wants to travel.

Using because

StructureExample
result + because + reasonI live here because it's quiet.

"Because" always introduces a reason — a full clause with its own subject and verb, not just a noun.

Grammar practice: complete each sentence with because

  1. giving a reason I live in the countryside it's beautiful.
  2. giving a reason She is tired she worked all night.
  3. giving a reason We stayed inside it was raining.
  4. giving a reason He studies English he wants to travel.
  5. giving a reason They moved their old house was too small.
  6. giving a reason I'm happy it's Friday.
  7. giving a reason She left early she felt sick.
  8. giving a reason We chose this house it has a big garden.

Reading practice

Diego walks to work because the office is close by. He doesn't own a car because he doesn't need one here. On weekends, he visits the market because the fresh food is wonderful. Diego is happy because he made the right choice.

Units 21–26

Speaking practice

Practice speaking like in a speaking exam such as IELTS. Part 1: answer short questions about you. Part 2: prepare for one minute, then talk about a topic for one to two minutes. Part 3: act out a conversation with a partner. Try first, then open the examples.

Part 1: Interview

Answer each question in one to three sentences. Don't just say "yes" or "no" — add a reason or an extra detail.

There is / there are

1. Is there a park near your home?

Show example answer
Yes, there is. There's a big park five minutes from my house.
There is / there are

2. What is there in your neighborhood?

Show example answer
There are some shops, a bakery, and two schools, but there isn't a cinema.
Any / some

3. Are there any good restaurants in your town?

Show example answer
Yes, there are some great pizza restaurants, but there aren't any Japanese restaurants.
Articles

4. What is in your bag right now?

Show example answer
There's a phone, a book, and an umbrella. The umbrella is small and red.
Imperatives

5. Tell me how to get from here to the nearest bus stop.

Show example answer
Go out of the building and turn left. Walk to the corner and turn right. The bus stop is next to the bank.
Adjectives

6. Describe your town in three adjectives.

Show example answer
My town is small, quiet, and friendly.
And / but

7. What do you like and not like about your home?

Show example answer
My apartment is bright and clean, but it's very small.
Because

8. Do you like your town? Why?

Show example answer
Yes, I do, because the people are friendly and it's very safe.

Part 2: Long turn

You have one minute to prepare. You can write some notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.

Describe your neighborhood.

You should say:

  • what there is in it
  • what the streets and buildings are like
  • what there isn't in it

and explain if you like living there and why.

0:00 Press a button to start
Show example answer
I live in a neighborhood called Vila Nova. It's near the center of the city. There are a lot of small shops, and there's a big supermarket on the main street. There are two schools and a beautiful old church. The streets are busy in the morning, but they are quiet at night. The buildings are old and colorful. There isn't a cinema, and there aren't any big parks, but there's a small square with trees. I like living here because my neighbors are friendly and everything is close to my house.

Part 3: Role-plays

Work with a partner. Student A and Student B read only their own card. Then have the conversation.

Asking for directions

Student A is a tourist. Student B lives in the town. You are both in front of the train station.

Student A

  • Ask if there is a bank near here.
  • Ask for directions to the bank.
  • Ask if there are any good cafés near the bank.
  • Say thank you.

Student B

  • Town information:
  • The bank is on Park Street, next to the post office.
  • From the station: turn left, walk to the second corner, turn right.
  • There are two cafés across the street from the bank.
Useful languageExcuse me, is there a… near here?How do I get to…?Turn left / right.Go straight.It's next to / across from…
Show example dialogue

A: Excuse me. Is there a bank near here?

B: Yes, there is. It's on Park Street.

A: How do I get there?

B: Turn left here and walk to the second corner. Then turn right. The bank is next to the post office.

A: Thanks. Are there any good cafés near the bank?

B: Yes, there are two cafés across the street. The small one is really nice.

A: Great! Thank you very much.

B: You're welcome. Have a nice day!

Choosing an apartment

Student A is a real estate agent. Student B is looking for an apartment.

Student A

  • Apartment information:
  • Two bedrooms, one bathroom
  • A big, bright living room
  • No balcony
  • Some shops and a bus stop nearby
  • Price: $900 a month

Student B

  • Ask how many bedrooms there are.
  • Ask what the living room is like.
  • Ask if there's a balcony.
  • Ask what there is near the apartment.
  • Decide: do you want it? Say why (because…).
Useful languageHow many… are there?Is there a…?What is the… like?I'd like it because…It's nice, but…
Show example dialogue

B: Hello. How many bedrooms are there?

A: There are two bedrooms and one bathroom.

B: What is the living room like?

A: It's big and very bright.

B: Is there a balcony?

A: No, there isn't, but there are some big windows.

B: What is there near the apartment?

A: There are some shops and a bus stop. The bus stop is very close.

B: How much is it?

A: It's nine hundred dollars a month.

B: It's a little expensive, but I like it because it's bright and near the bus stop. I'll take it!

Writing practice

Read the task, plan your ideas, and write your text in the box. The counter shows how many words you have — it turns green when you're in the right range. Use the grammar from these units. When you finish, compare your text with the example.

Task 1: A note for a house sitter

Note40–60 words

A friend is staying in your home this weekend. Write a note with instructions.

Write about

  • what your friend should do (feed the cat, water the plants…)
  • what your friend shouldn't do
  • where some things are (There is / There are…)

Try to use

  • imperatives (Feed…, Close…, Don't…)
  • there is / there are
  • some / any
0 words
Show example text (55 words)
Hi Marta, Thank you for staying here! Please feed the cat twice a day. There is some cat food in the kitchen. Water the plants on Saturday. Don't open the window in the bedroom, because the cat likes to jump out. There are some eggs and some bread in the fridge for you. Enjoy! Luis

Task 2: My town

Description70–90 words

Write a description of your town or city for a travel website.

Write about

  • what there is in your town
  • what there isn't
  • what your town is like (adjectives)
  • why people should visit (because…)

Try to use

  • there is / there are / there isn't / there aren't any
  • a / an / the
  • adjectives
  • and / but / because
0 words
Show example text (78 words)
My town is small, but it's very beautiful. There is an old castle on a hill, and there are some great restaurants in the main square. There's a river, and there are boats for tourists. There isn't an airport, but there's a train station with trains to the city every hour. The people are friendly and the food is delicious. Visit my town in the summer, because the weather is warm and there are a lot of festivals!
